The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording

The Build OrderPart 9

By lowob · 1 August 2026 · 10-minute read · Revenue

The record is the part of the brain a company must own, and it pays back fastest where decisions are frequent, similar, quickly graded and later defended. On the commercial line, ten decision classes meet that test, from discount exceptions and lead qualification to campaign spend and closed-lost reasons. Each record needs five fields (the decision, its reason, owner, status, and an expected outcome with a date to check), plus a sixth, the outcome, written back when it arrives. Start with one class, not ten.

Every firm loses deals for reasons it has seen before. A pitch is lost on price; six months later a similar pitch is lost the same way. Nobody connects the two, because neither decision was recorded anywhere a person or an agent could find it. The context layer can now retrieve the proposal, the emails and the invoice. It cannot retrieve a reason nobody wrote down.

This is the record layer, the half of the brain we argue a company must own (Buy context, own judgment). The question is which decisions deserve a record. Recording everything creates a filing burden nobody maintains. Recording nothing leaves the reasoning layer guessing.

Which decisions deserve a record

We published the test in Where judgment arrives first: a decision layer earns its keep first where decisions are frequent, similar to past cases, graded quickly by an outcome, and later defended by someone accountable. Gartner has forecast that at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agentic AI by 2028; the decisions that get there first will be the ones with a record behind them.

The ten commercial decisions

#Decision classTypical frequencyOutcome known withinWho defends it
1Discount or price exceptionWeeklyOne sales cycleFinance and head of sales
2Qualify or drop an inbound leadDailyWeeksHead of sales
3Pursue or pass on a pitch or RFPWeeklyOne sales cycleLeadership
4Pricing a proposalWeeklyOne sales cycleAccount owner and finance
5Campaign spend and reallocationMonthlyA quarterBudget holder
6Partner or channel selectionQuarterlyTwo quartersRevenue leader
7Account prioritisation for the quarterQuarterlyA quarterRevenue leader
8Approving a public or marketing claimWeeklyWeeks, or at auditMarketing and compliance
9Follow-up timing and next step on key dealsDailyWeeksAccount owner
10Why a deal was won or lostWeeklyAlready knownHead of sales

The list is deliberately commercial and deliberately ordinary. These are the calls a mid-size firm makes every week and rarely writes down. Three of them (discount exceptions, pursue or pass, and win-loss reasons) recur so often and grade so quickly that they will show patterns within a single quarter.

What each record must hold

In The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind we set out the core of a useful record: the decision, the reason and owner, and what changed. In The field that makes a record a judgment and Supersede, never overwrite we added the fields that let a system learn. For the commercial line, five fields are the minimum, and the sixth arrives later.

FieldExample (discount exception)Why it matters
DecisionApprove 12% off list for a two-year termWhat was decided, in one line
ReasonCompeting quote at a lower price; strategic logo in a new sectorWhat the reasoning layer will retrieve as precedent
OwnerHead of salesOne accountable person
StatusCurrent, superseded or reversedStops old guidance being treated as current
Expected outcome and check dateWin within 30 days; renewal at full price in two yearsMakes the decision gradable
Outcome (written back)Won; renewal pendingTurns the record into evidence

The last two rows are what make a log into a judgment record. Without an expected outcome there is nothing to compare the result with. Without the written-back outcome there is nothing to learn from.

A decision without an expected outcome cannot be graded, and a decision that cannot be graded cannot be learned from.

Where the record should live

Choose the place already open when the decision is made.

OptionGood forWatch for
A custom object or fields in the CRMDiscounts, pursue or pass, win-lossKeep it to the six fields; avoid free text only
A shared table (Airtable, a sheet, a database)Campaign spend, partner selection, prioritisationNeeds a clear owner and an export path
A document workspace (Notion or similar)Claims approvals with attached evidenceStructure must stay consistent enough to query

Whichever you choose, apply the three tests from Buy context, own judgment: can every record and its history be exported in a documented format, will it survive a change of vendor, and does the company control retention and deletion?

The capture habit

Records fail when they depend on memory. Attach capture to moments that already exist:

  • At approval. A discount or price exception cannot be approved without its reason and expected outcome.
  • At stage change. Moving a deal to won or lost requires the reason.
  • At the weekly review. Pursue-or-pass and prioritisation calls are recorded in the meeting, not after it.
  • At the check date. The owner gets a reminder to record the outcome.

The data shows why capture must be designed rather than requested. Validity's 2025 survey found 37% of CRM users reporting revenue lost to poor data quality, and 37% reporting colleagues fabricating data to satisfy decision-makers. Records filled in to satisfy a review are worse than no records.

Start with one class

Pick one decision class whose outcome shows within a quarter and record it properly for 90 days. Discount exceptions and closed-lost reasons are the usual choices because both are frequent, already partly captured in the CRM, and defended by someone who cares about the answer. After 90 days, look at the outcomes against the expectations. The first uncomfortable finding is usually the moment the build stops being an IT project.

Illustrative example: recording discount exceptions
Decision
Record every discount beyond the standard tier with its reason, owner, expected outcome and a 30-day check.
Reason and owner
Discounts were rising with no evidence they improved win rates. Owned by the head of sales.
What changed
After a quarter, discounts in two service lines show no higher win rate than standard pricing; the rule for those lines is tightened and reviewed again in a quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size services business, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Record decisions, not everything. Ten commercial classes pass the test; most of what a team does does not need a record.
  • Six fields. Decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back.
  • Capture at moments that already exist. Approvals, stage changes, weekly reviews and check dates.
  • Start with one class for 90 days. Usually discount exceptions or closed-lost reasons.
Gateway card

Gateway 2 begins here

  • One decision class chosen
  • Six fields defined and required at the moment of decision
  • Expected outcome and check date on every record
  • Outcomes written back on schedule
  • A value at stake recorded, so the build can report in money

Common questions

What is a decision record?

A structured entry for an important decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, whether it is current, what outcome was expected and when to check, and later what actually happened.

Which sales decisions should be recorded?

Those that are frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended: discount and price exceptions, lead qualification, pursue-or-pass on pitches, proposal pricing, campaign spend, partner selection, account prioritisation, claims approvals, follow-up timing on key deals, and win-loss reasons.

Where should decision records live?

Where the decision is made: CRM fields for deal decisions, a shared table for budget and partner decisions, or a document workspace for claims with evidence. Records must be exportable.

How does a decision record help AI agents?

Agents can read comparable past decisions as precedent before acting, and outcomes written back to records let the system learn which reasoning worked.

Sources and notes

  • Gartner forecast on autonomous work decisions, June 2025, as reported by W.Media.
  • Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2025, and MediaPost coverage. Survey of 602 CRM users.

Next move

Pick one of the ten decisions and look at the last ten times your team made it. How many have a written reason, and how many have a known outcome? That gap is the first thing to close.
